# Two boundary rows, a cubic inequality, and arbitrary triangle cuts
new stochastic-matrix mechanism and the complete transfer to an ordinary
triangle. The separate all-stochastic-matrix extremum proof is in
`candidate 6b3596acb8604c8b`.
No assertion about arbitrary ordinary convex bodies or OC follows here.

## 1. Row functional

For a nonnegative triple v, sort its entries as x<=y<=z and define

    phi(v)^2=z(x+y)-xy.

Equivalently this square is the maximum of the three quadratics
v_j(v_k+v_l)-v_k v_l. It is nonnegative and at most z^2, since it equals
z^2-(z-x)(z-y). Thus phi is continuous, homogeneous, and at most the
largest entry. These facts include all zero and tied-entry cases.

For a nonnegative column-stochastic three-by-three matrix X, write
F_i=phi(X_i)^2. The desired cubic is

    sum_i F_i+2 sqrt(F_1 F_2 F_3)<=1.                 (1)

## 2. Complete boundary lemma

Assume at least two rows of X each have a zero entry. Row and column
permutations do not affect the assertion.

If two chosen zeros are in the same column, write the columns as
(0,0,1), (a,b,c), (p,q,r). All entries are nonnegative and the latter
two columns sum to one. Then

    F_1=ap, F_2=bq, F_3=c+r-cr<=1.

The last formula uses that the first entry of the third row is one,
hence is a largest entry. Expanding the column sums gives

    F_1+F_2+F_3=1-(aq+bp).

By AM--GM, aq+bp>=2 sqrt(abpq)>=2 sqrt(F_1 F_2 F_3). This proves (1),
including all zero entries.

Otherwise choose the two zeros in different columns and write

    X = [[0,a,b], [c,0,e], [r,s,t]],
    a=1-s, c=1-r, b+e=L=1-t.

All variables lie in [0,1]. The first two row squares are ab and ce.
For the third put F=phi(r,s,t)^2 and

    B=(s+t-st)(r+t-rt)=(1-aL)(1-cL).

The differences between B and the three candidate quadratics for F are
respectively

    t(1-r)[t(1-s)+2s],
    t(1-s)[t(1-r)+2r],
    t^2(1-r)(1-s)+2rs(1-t).

Each is nonnegative, so F<=B. If L=0, then b=e=0 and (1) is simply
F<=1. Suppose L>0. Consider the symmetric matrix

    A = [[a,sqrt(acF)], [sqrt(acF),c]].

The matrix (1-F)I-LA is PSD. Indeed its determinant is exactly

    (1-F)[(1-aL)(1-cL)-F]>=0,

and its diagonal entries are nonnegative: the bound on F gives

    1-F>=L(a+c-acL)>=L max(a,c).

Here the last inequality follows from a,c,L in [0,1]. Therefore, using
the vector (sqrt(b),sqrt(e)), whose squared norm is L,

    ab+ce+2sqrt(abceF)
       <=(1-F)(b+e)/L=1-F.

This is (1). The proof needs no positivity, distinct maximum, or source
calibration assumption. It covers every matrix with the stated two zeros.

## 3. The exact one-row variational identity

Let Xi be uniform barycentric coordinates on a triangle, and let
G_v(h)=P(v dot Xi<=h). For a nonnegative triple v,

    inf_{h>0, G_v(h)>0} h/sqrt(G_v(h))=phi(v).       (2)

For x<y<z the elementary vertex-cap area formulas are

    G(h)=(h-x)^2/[(y-x)(z-x)]          for x<=h<=y,
    G(h)=1-(z-h)^2/[(z-x)(z-y)]        for y<=h<=z,
    G(h)=1                           for h>=z.

The first ratio is nonincreasing, strictly decreasing if x>0. On the
second interval, its derivative vanishes at

    h_*=x+y-xy/z,

which lies in [y,z]. Its derivative is negative before and positive
after h_*, as follows by differentiating G-hG'/2. The squared value at
h_* is z h_*=z(x+y)-xy. For x=0 the first ratio is constant and gives
the same answer. The cases x=y or y=z follow by direct substitution in
the remaining nonempty interval; for a constant row the answer is z.
For the zero row both sides of (2) vanish. These observations also cover
(0,0,z), where the infimum is approached as h decreases to zero.

In particular, at any interior threshold with 0<G(h)<1 satisfying
hG'(h)=2G(h), the ratio in (2) is a global minimum. The area profile is
differentiable at a middle vertex value in dimension two, so this statement
also includes a cutting line through a vertex.

## 4. Transfer to a triangle with any three balanced cuts

Let T be an ordinary planar triangle of area V>0, let y be in its
interior, and let u_1,u_2,u_3 be nonzero spanning normals with
u_1+u_2+u_3=0. Let

    Q_i=|T intersect {u_i dot (x-y)>=0}|/V,
    S_i=length(T intersect {u_i dot (x-y)=0})/(|u_i| V),
    M=sum_i Q_i/S_i.

All Q_i lie strictly between zero and one, and all S_i and M are positive.
Let P_j be the triangle vertices, t_ij=u_i dot(P_j-y), and let E_ij be
the fraction of the edge opposite P_j captured by the i-th halfspace.
The divergence theorem for the field x-P_j on the captured triangle
portion gives

    E_ij=Q_i-t_ij S_i/2.                            (3)

For completeness, the flux through the two edges incident to P_j is zero;
the full opposite-edge flux is 2V, so its captured flux is 2V E_ij.
The cut's outward normal is -u_i/|u_i|, giving flux t_ij V S_i.
The divergence is two. Rearranging the resulting identity proves (3),
including cuts through vertices, whose zero-length boundary pieces add
no flux.

Set

    a_i=Q_i/(S_i M),       X_ij=E_ij/(S_i M).

The matrix X is nonnegative. Equation (3) and balanced normals give
sum_i X_ij=sum_i a_i-sum_i t_ij/(2M)=1. Thus it is column stochastic.
For a uniform point of T with barycentric vector Xi,

    X_i dot Xi=a_i-u_i dot(x-y)/(2M).

Consequently its distribution function G_i satisfies

    G_i(a_i)=Q_i,       G_i'(a_i)=2M S_i,
    a_i G_i'(a_i)=2Q_i.

By (2), phi(X_i)=a_i/sqrt(Q_i). Define the ordinary row vector

    f_i=2sqrt(Q_i)/(S_i M)=2phi(X_i).

The all-stochastic-matrix theorem from the companion source therefore
gives

    f_1^2+f_2^2+f_3^2+f_1 f_2 f_3<=4.              (4)

No assumption was made about how many vertices a cap captures or whether
its boundary passes through a vertex. All three caps are closed, and all
their boundaries have zero ordinary area. The normalization agrees exactly
with the raw-area definition f_i=2sqrt(V Q_i^raw)/(S_i^raw M).

This extends the triangle cubic from strict distinct-vertex incidence to
every balanced spanning three-cut circuit on a planar triangle. In
combination with the independently audited spectral reduction it removes
triangular witnesses without any cap ceiling. Quadrilateral witnesses
still require a separate proof or counterexample to this stronger cubic.
